title: Experimental Investigation of a Hybrid Thermal Management System for <scp>LFP</scp> Battery Packs Using <scp> Ag <sub>2</sub> O </scp> Nano Fluid–Cooled Serpentine Copper Tubes Embedded in Graphite‐Enhanced <scp>PCM</scp>
abstract: ABSTRACT Effective thermal management is critical to ensure the safety, reliability, and performance of lithium‐ion battery modules under high thermal loads. While hybrid phase change material (PCM)–liquid cooling systems have been widely explored, the present study introduces a novel material‐level enhancement through the use of an Ag 2 O–ethylene glycol Nano fluid, whose application in battery thermal management remains largely unexplored. A compact 4S5P battery module comprising 21 700‐type lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells (14 V, 22.5 Ah) is experimentally investigated under 1C, 1.5C, and 2C discharge rates, along with 1C charging conditions. The proposed hybrid BTMS integrates PCM with active liquid cooling using Ag 2 O Nano fluid at varying concentrations (1–5 wt.%), enabling a systematic evaluation of its thermo‐physical impact. The results demonstrate that, in the absence of thermal management, the module temperature rapidly increases to approximately 60°C at 2C, indicating severe thermal stress. In contrast, the proposed system significantly enhances heat dissipation, maintaining the maximum cell temperature within 30°C–32°C, thereby achieving a reduction of 5%. Furthermore, increasing nanoparticle concentration improves convective heat transfer, with optimal performance observed at 5 wt.%, reaching temperature to 29°C resulting in improved temperature uniformity across the module. Results demonstrate the effectiveness of Ag 2 O nanofluid relative to base fluid under the investigated operating conditions. This study not only demonstrates the feasibility of Ag 2 O‐based Nano fluids in BTMS but also provides a scalable and high‐performance thermal management solution for high‐power cylindrical battery modules in electric vehicles and energy storage systems.

title: Low‐Temperature Experimental Characterization of Magnetite‐Based Rock‐Bed Thermal Battery
abstract: ABSTRACT Rock bed thermal energy storage (RTES) systems are increasingly used as affordable and scalable solutions for low‐temperature heat storage. However, experimental investigations of magnetite packed beds under repeated charge–discharge cycles remain limited. This study experimentally evaluates the thermal performance of a horizontal cylindrical RTES system filled with magnetite and operated as a low‐temperature thermal battery for greenhouse applications. Two airflow strategies are compared over two successive cycles of charging and discharging: (i) unidirectional airflow during both charging and discharging (Model 1) and (ii) reversed airflow during discharge (Model 2). Thermal performance is analyzed through temperature stratification, heat transfer dynamics, energy recovery, and dimensionless performance indicators, including the Thermal Efficiency Index ( TEI ), Temperature Uniformity Index ( TUI ), Normalized Temperature Standard Deviation ( NTSD ), and Temperature Gradient Ratio ( TGR ). Results show that airflow reversal significantly enhances thermal propagation and heat extraction. Model 2 achieves a more pronounced thermal‐front response, generally higher TUI and TGR values, and higher energy recovery, delivering up to 30% more recovered heat during the first discharge period and approximately 15.79% more during the second discharge period compared with Model 1. Moreover, Model 2 exhibits higher TEI values across the investigated operating periods, with particularly noticeable advantages during the first discharge and second charging periods. These findings demonstrate that discharge flow reversal is an effective operating strategy for improving the responsiveness and heat‐recovery performance of low‐temperature magnetite RTES systems.

title: Physics-inspired degradation modeling guided by dynamic orbits for battery health prognostics
abstract: Remaining useful life (RUL) prediction must be reliable for optimal operation, maintenance scheduling and lifecycle management of battery-powered systems. In practical applications, batteries are frequently subjected to fluctuating power demands and irregular operating schedules, resulting in condition-dependent capacity variations that can obscure the underlying slow degradation trend and challenge conventional RUL prediction methods. Building on the experimentally observed orbit-like degradation behavior under dynamic operating conditions, this study develops a physics-inspired degradation modeling framework, termed PhyOrbitNet, for battery RUL prediction. PhyOrbitNet jointly represents intra-cycle degradation manifestation and cross-cycle degradation propagation. In the feature learning stage, a mathematical framework is derived to describe the coupled evolution of fast-varying observables and slow-varying degradation variables in a high-dimensional phase space, and is reformulated as a cross-attention module within the Transformer architecture. Furthermore, considering the influence of historical degradation information, the dual form of a state-space model is derived and formulated as structured masked attention. A knowledge distillation mechanism is further introduced to transfer degradation representation capability to a student model driven solely by operating conditions, enabling long-term RUL prediction. Experimental results demonstrate that PhyOrbitNet provides accurate RUL prediction across different cells and lifetime stages under dynamic operating conditions.
title_zh: Physics-inspired degradation modeling guided by dynamic orbits for battery health prognostics

title: Domain adaptation state of health estimation for lithium-ion batteries accounting for state of charge dependence
abstract: Accurate State of Health (SOH) estimation is essential for ensuring the safety, reliability, and long-term performance of electric vehicle batteries. However, the generalization performance of Artificial Intelligence methods depends on the quality and coverage of training data. Acquiring high-quality labeled data with sufficient coverage remains a challenge. To address this, this paper first comprehensively compares and analyzes the State of Charge (SOC) dependence of the mechanical, electrical, and thermal features of batteries under different initial SOC. Features with weak SOC dependence are selected as model inputs, enabling robust SOH estimation in partial charge–discharge scenarios using only fully completed charge–discharge data. This effectively reduces the model’s demand for broad data coverage. Then, this paper proposes a domain adaptation method based on Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD), which integrates the Transformer and Kolmogorov–Arnold Network (KAN). Experimental results show that adopting features with weak SOC dependence reduces the relative Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) by 85.48% for slow charging and 64.33% for fast charging. Moreover, the proposed domain adaptation method achieves a 47.69% relative reduction in MAPE.
title_zh: Domain adaptation state of health estimation for lithium-ion batteries accounting for state of charge dependence

title: AGLFormer: Compact feature selection and parameter-budget-aware global-local modeling for lithium-ion battery state-of-health estimation
abstract: Accurate state-of-health (SOH) estimation is essential for lithium-ion battery management, while practical deployment requires an appropriate balance among input compactness, prediction accuracy, model capacity, and performance stability. This study proposes a deployment-aware SOH estimation framework based on an Adaptive Global-Local Former (AGLFormer). In the feature-engineering stage, statistical health features are extracted from charging profiles and ranked using an equally weighted combination of the Pearson and Spearman correlation coefficients. Four nested feature subsets, namely FS-1, FS-25, FS-50, and FS-100, are subsequently constructed to investigate the effect of feature quantity on SOH prediction performance. In the prediction stage, AGLFormer combines convolution-enhanced linear attention with an adaptive multi-scale feed-forward network to model global degradation dependencies and local degradation variations. Experiments on the CALCE and Oxford datasets show that increasing the number of input features does not consistently improve prediction accuracy. FS-25 achieves the best validation performance on CALCE, whereas the more compact FS-1 performs best on Oxford, demonstrating that an appropriately compact feature subset can maintain or improve prediction accuracy, enhance the reachability of high-accuracy results across different hyperparameter configurations, and reduce feature-extraction and data-preprocessing overhead. Compared with long short-term memory (LSTM), Transformer, convolutional neural network–Transformer (CNN-Transformer), iTransformer, and ModernTCN, AGLFormer achieves the best average performance on both datasets. Its average R 2 , mean absolute error (MAE), root mean square error (RMSE), and mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) are 0.9886, 0.0143, 0.0206, and 0.0250 on CALCE and 0.9943, 0.0028, 0.0035, and 0.0034 on Oxford, respectively. Parameter-budget analysis further shows that AGLFormer achieves the best overall budget-matched performance on both datasets, with consistent advantages on Oxford and capacity-dependent gains on CALCE. These results demonstrate that the proposed framework provides a favorable balance among feature compactness, prediction accuracy, performance stability, and model capacity for lithium-ion battery SOH estimation.
title_zh: AGLFormer: Compact feature selection and parameter-budget-aware global-local modeling for lithium-ion battery state-of-health estimation
